implementation_notes: Since C++20 the standard library ships the semaphore the pattern needs: one std::counting_semaphore<N> per dependency (std::binary_semaphore for a single slot), try_acquire_for() as a bounded wait that doubles as the fail-fast path, and a RAII guard whose destructor releases the permit so every exit path returns it - replacing the classic explicit pool bookkeeping with scope-based release. Keep this form when calls suspend or an event loop already owns the threads; switch to the dedicated-pool variant when the dependency call blocks a thread.

variants.name: std::counting_semaphore permit (C++20)
variants.implementation_notes: Since C++20 the standard library ships the semaphore the pattern needs: one std::counting_semaphore<N> per dependency (std::binary_semaphore for a single slot), try_acquire_for() as a bounded wait that doubles as the fail-fast path, and a RAII guard whose destructor releases the permit so every exit path returns it - replacing the classic explicit pool bookkeeping with scope-based release. Keep this form when calls suspend or an event loop already owns the threads; switch to the dedicated-pool variant when the dependency call blocks a thread.
pitfalls: std::counting_semaphore exists only from C++20; older toolchains need a mutex/condition_variable counter or a library semaphore (Boost).
try_acquire_for returns false both on timeout and on saturation by other callers; the rejection is the same, but logs should not claim a specific cause.
A counting semaphore does not bound the waiting queue, so unconstrained waiters still grow memory and latency unless waits are timed out.
Never capture the semaphore by value in the guard: the release must hit the shared instance, not a copy.

variants.name: Dedicated fixed worker pool per dependency (C++11)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic thread-level bulkhead: a fixed pool of N threads per dependency plus a bounded queue; the caller posts work and never blocks, so a stalled dependency occupies only its own N threads. Boost.Asio's thread_pool is the pragmatic library form and a hand-rolled std::thread pool over std::condition_variable the dependency-free one. Choose this over the semaphore when the dependency call blocks a thread and the caller must stay responsive; remember the pool's work queue is unbounded until you bound it yourself.
pitfalls: boost::asio::thread_pool's work queue is unbounded; without a separate admission bound a stalled dependency accumulates arbitrary pending work.
Captured state must outlive the posted functor: capturing stack references by reference is a use-after-free when the caller returns first.
One pool per dependency multiplies idle threads and stacks; never create a pool per request or per call site.
std::counting_semaphore exists only from C++20; older toolchains need a mutex/condition_variable counter or a library semaphore (Boost).
try_acquire_for returns false both on timeout and on saturation by other callers; the rejection is the same, but logs should not claim a specific cause.
A counting semaphore does not bound the waiting queue, so unconstrained waiters still grow memory and latency unless waits are timed out.
Never capture the semaphore by value in the guard: the release must hit the shared instance, not a copy.
